characters: Children in school uniforms greeting a teacher, an elder and a neighbour at sunrise, midday and sunset.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm voice; the Twi greetings are said slowly and clearly, with the children repeating
narrationPlan.pace: Warm and clear, with a pause for the greeting words (about 70 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A cheerful clapping song with three short tunes, one for each part of the day (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Greetings matter in Ghanaian life, and children are taught to greet elders. Maakye, Maaha, Maadwo and Akwaaba are Twi (Akan). Other languages, such as Ga, Ewe, Dagbani and Fante, have their own greetings and teachers should invite children to share these.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have a Twi speaker confirm Maakye (good morning), Maaha (good afternoon), Maadwo (good evening) and Akwaaba (welcome), and their spelling.
Check that the song does not suggest that Twi is the only language of Ghana.

teacherGuide.overview: A greetings song that pairs English and Twi greetings with the time of day. Form: five couplets. Rhyming pairs: here/near, high/by, red/bed, in/grin, grace/face. It builds manners, home-language pride and respect.
learningGoals: Say the greetings for morning, afternoon and evening.
Respect the home languages in the room.
beforeReading: Ask: how do you greet people at home? What do you say?
whileReading: Teach the Twi greetings slowly and have children echo them.
afterReading: Role-play greeting a teacher, an elder and a visitor.
Make a greetings chart with the children’s home languages.
discussion: What do we say when we meet someone in the morning?
reflection: Who will you greet kindly today?

support: Use pictures of a sunrise, a noon sun and a sunset to link the greeting to the time.
stretch: Teach the class a greeting from another Ghanaian language and add a verse.

culturalNotes: Greetings matter in Ghanaian life, and children are taught to greet elders. Maakye, Maaha, Maadwo and Akwaaba are Twi (Akan). Other languages, such as Ga, Ewe, Dagbani and Fante, have their own greetings and teachers should invite children to share these.
localiseThis: Replace the Twi words with greetings in the local language of your school, if different.
Invite a parent or elder to teach their greeting.
